title_en: Why the Sea Rises and Falls
description_ru: Объяснение приливов и отливов: роль Луны, Солнца и вращения Земли, а также почему в некоторых местах вода поднимается на несколько этажей.
text:
Anyone who has spent a day at the seaside knows that the water does not stay in one place. In the morning, the beach may be wide and dry, and by the afternoon the waves are lapping at the wall. This daily rhythm, which has been observed since ancient times, is caused by tides, and the main reason for them is the Moon. Yet the explanation is more subtle than most people imagine, and it involves some surprising ideas about gravity.

Gravity is a force that pulls objects towards each other, and it becomes weaker with distance. The Moon pulls on the whole Earth, but it pulls harder on the side that faces it than on the side that faces away. The solid planet cannot move much in response, but the oceans are fluid, so the water on the near side is drawn towards the Moon and forms a gentle bulge. That much is easy to accept.

What is harder to believe is that a second bulge forms on the opposite side of the planet at the same time. The best way to understand it is to remember that the Earth and the Moon actually orbit around a common point, a little like two skaters spinning while they hold hands. The Earth's centre is pulled slightly more strongly than the water on the far side, so the water is, in effect, left behind. The result is that there are two bulges of water, one facing the Moon and one pointing away from it.

As the Earth rotates once every twenty-four hours, any coastline passes through both bulges, which means that most places experience two high tides and two low tides each day. The interval is not exactly twelve hours, however, because the Moon is moving in its orbit as well. It takes about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes for the Moon to appear in the same position in the sky, so the tides arrive, on average, about fifty minutes later each day. Fishermen and sailors have always been forced to keep this in mind.

The Sun also has an influence, although it is much weaker, in spite of its enormous size. It is so far away that its pull on the oceans is less than half of the Moon's. When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are lined up, which happens at new moon and full moon, the two effects are combined, and the tides are unusually large. These are called spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season and comes from an old word meaning to jump. About a week later, when the Sun and the Moon pull at right angles, the tides are smaller, and they are known as neap tides.

The shape of the coast makes an enormous difference. In the open ocean, the tide rises by only about half a metre, and in the Mediterranean Sea, which is nearly closed, it is barely noticeable. But where the water is funnelled into a long, narrowing bay, it can be pushed to extraordinary heights. The Bay of Fundy in Canada is famous for tides of up to sixteen metres, which is roughly the height of a five-storey building. Fishing boats there are left sitting on the mud at low tide, and a few hours later they float high above the harbour wall.

Tides are not only a curiosity. They create rich habitats in the intertidal zone, the strip of shore that is covered and uncovered every day. Animals living there, such as crabs, mussels and barnacles, must be able to survive both underwater and in the open air, and many of them have developed shells that seal in moisture. Some species even time their breeding to the tides, so that their young are released when the water is at its highest.

People have also learned to use the tides. For centuries, tide mills ground grain in Europe, and today a few power stations generate electricity from the flow of water in and out of estuaries. Unlike the wind or the sun, the tide is perfectly predictable, and the times of high and low water can be calculated years in advance. That reliability is also a reason why the tables published for harbours are among the oldest scientific documents still in everyday use.

There is one more curious consequence. The friction caused by the tides is slowly braking the Earth's rotation, and the energy is being transferred to the Moon, which moves away from us by about three and a half centimetres every year. Millions of years ago, days were shorter and the Moon was closer. In the very distant future, our satellite will be so far away that it will no longer be able to cause a total eclipse of the Sun. For now, however, the sea continues to rise and fall, reminding us that the Earth is part of a larger system.

questions.question: What is the main cause of tides?
How many high tides do most places have each day?
What are spring tides?
questions.answer: Unusually large tides when the Sun, Moon and Earth are lined up.

questions.question: Where does the Moon move each year?
questions.answer: It moves away from Earth by about three and a half centimetres.
